record.original_question: For a fixed positive integer k, what is the minimum number of kth powers needed so that every positive integer can be represented as a sum of that many kth powers?

evidence.quote: Waring proposed a problem of finding the minimum number of kth powers necessary to express every positive integer as a sum of powers.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For a fixed integer $k \geq 2$, let $g(k)$ denote the smallest positive integer $s$ such that every positive integer $n$ can be written as a sum of at most $s$ nonnegative $k$-th powers, i.e., $n = x_1^k + x_2^k + \cdots + x_s^k$ with $x_i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$. Determine $g(k)$ as an explicit function of $k$.

It is classical that $g(2)=4$, $g(3)=9$, $g(4)=19$, $g(5)=37$. Define
$$ I(k) = 2^k + \left\lfloor (3/2)^k \right\rfloor - 2. $$
Prove that $g(k) = I(k)$ for every integer $k \geq 2$, or otherwise determine the exact value of $g(k)$. Equivalently, show that for every integer $k \geq 2$ one has
$$ \{(3/2)^k\} \leq 1 - (3/4)^k, $$
where $\{x\}$ denotes the fractional part of $x$, since this inequality is known to imply $g(k) = I(k)$.
artifact.status_search_result: The function $g(k)$ has been computed exactly for all sufficiently large $k$: results of Dickson, Pillai, Rubugunday, and Niven (1936–1944) prove $g(k) = 2^k + \lfloor (3/2)^k \rfloor - 2$ whenever $\{(3/2)^k\} \leq 1 - (3/4)^k$. Mahler (1957) proved this inequality holds for all sufficiently large $k$, and Kubina–Wunderlich (1990) verified it computationally up to $k = 471{,}600{,}000$. Thus $g(k)$ is known for every $k$ in this range, but a fully unconditional proof for all $k$ remains open because Mahler's result is ineffective.

status_evidence.title: Waring's problem - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: g(k) = 2^k + floor((3/2)^k) - 2 has been verified for 6 ≤ k ≤ 471,600,000 by Kubina and Wunderlich; Mahler proved it for all sufficiently large k.
status_evidence.claim: Formula for g(k) verified for k up to ~4.7×10^8 and for all sufficiently large k, but not unconditionally for every k.
